engine.title: Stop buying strength that has already run
engine.body: The 4H RSI ceiling for longs was 75. Splitting every closed trade by the RSI recorded at entry showed the engine bleeding above 65 and profitable below it. The ceiling is now 65.
engine.note: Holds in both halves of the sample and at every cut point tested (60, 65, 70), so it is not one lucky threshold. The threshold was still chosen from this sample, so treat the size as an upper bound.

engine.title: A break-even stop would not have helped
engine.body: The median losing trade was +1.44R in profit before it reversed, and 59% touched a full +1R first. That looks like an obvious fix: move the stop to entry once price pays 1R. Re-walking every trade bar by bar, with winners subject to the same rule, says otherwise.
engine.note: The first version of this test only altered losers, which guarantees a positive answer. Correcting it reversed the conclusion. Nothing tested cleared one standard error, so no stop rule was adopted.

engine.title: Trades were being closed at prices that never traded
engine.body: The grader had never resolved a single trade — an exception was being swallowed silently — leaving a fallback path that could book an exit at a bar from before the signal existed. Every closed trade was re-graded against bars that actually printed.
evidence: exits corrected to a real price
engine.note: This moved the headline number against me. It is published anyway, because the earlier number was not real. Pre-correction data is kept in the repo rather than deleted.

engine.title: A first target must pay back the risk
engine.body: T1 was whichever structural level sat nearest the entry, with no distance test. One signal shipped a T1 worth 0.19R against its own stop, printed beside an R:R of 2.41 quoted off T2. T1 must now return at least 1R.

chess.title: Opening Principle #1: Control the Centre
chess.body: Place pawns on e4/d4 (White) or e5/d5 (Black). Pieces control more squares from the centre. A pawn on e4 controls d5 and f5. A pawn on the edge controls only 1 square. Open with 1.e4 or 1.d4 and you immediately claim space. This is the foundation of all chess strategy.

wisdom.title: Wisdom from Fathers Before You
wisdom.body: Your father had flaws. His father did too. But they also gave you things you don't yet see. The goal isn't to be a perfect father — it's to be a slightly more conscious one. Break the patterns you don't want to pass on. Keep the ones that built you. Each generation improves a little. That's legacy.

book.author: Atul Gawande
book.chapter: Checklists Are Not for Dumb People. They're for Experts.
book.lesson: Surgeon Atul Gawande studied why brilliant surgeons and pilots make elementary errors. The answer: not incompetence but complexity. Modern tasks have too many steps for any brain to hold reliably under pressure. His solution, borrowed from aviation: checklists. A two-minute surgical checklist reduced surgical complications by 36% and deaths by 47% in a global study. The lesson for knowledge work: expertise does not eliminate the need for process discipline. The most error-prone moments are not the hard parts of a task — they're the routine parts where experts assume they can proceed from memory. They can't.
book.key_quote: Checklists are not about distrust of expertise. They are about respecting the limits of human memory under pressure.
book.action: Identify your most error-prone recurring process (month-end close, financial review). Write a checklist for it this week. Use it next time.
crux: Failure in complex work is usually not ignorance. It is ineptitude — knowing what to do and not doing it.
Volume and complexity of knowledge now exceed what any individual can reliably hold in working memory.
Checklists convert known steps into guaranteed steps.
Two failure types: errors of ignorance (we don't know) and errors of ineptitude (we know but slipped). Checklists kill the second.
Good checklists are short — 5 to 9 items, one page, pause points at natural breaks.
Bad checklists are long, vague, and try to spell out every step. They get ignored.
DO-CONFIRM (act, then verify) versus READ-DO (read each line, then act). Pick deliberately.
Checklists must be tested in the real setting. Desk-designed lists fail in the field.
The largest gain is often communication: forcing names, roles, and concerns to be stated aloud.
A five-item surgical checklist cut deaths 47% and complications 36% across eight hospitals.
Experts resist checklists because they feel insulting. That reaction is the reason they are needed.
Discipline is harder than brilliance, and rarer.
learnings: Skill does not protect against the routine slip. Structure does.
The resistance to a checklist is ego, and ego is expensive.
Writing the list down is what converts intention into reliability.
Forcing people to speak up is a safety feature, not politeness.
examples: Boeing's Model 299 crashed in 1935 because pilots forgot one lock. A one-page checklist let the B-17 fly 1.8 million miles without a similar accident.
Johns Hopkins used a five-line central-line checklist and cut infection rates from 11% to zero over a year.
Van Halen's brown-M&M clause was a checklist canary: if the M&Ms were unsorted, the rigging had not been read either.
adapt: Pre-post checklist for Instagram: score the caption, check restricted terms, confirm no financial-advice phrasing. Five items, one screen.
Pre-deploy checklist: type-check, lint, verify which Vercel project the alias actually points at.
Month-end close checklist. Same order every month. Speed comes from the order, not from hurrying.
Pre-trade checklist: regime, stop distance versus ATR, position already open? The 59 duplicate NATGAS rows were an ineptitude error, not an ignorance one.

minimalism.title: The Uniform
minimalism.body: Pick a small set of clothes that always work and buy multiples. Ends the morning decision, ends the mismatched purchase, ends the wardrobe that is 80% unworn.
minimalism.action: Define your uniform in one sentence. Buy toward it, not around it.
minimalism.label: Minimalism

etiquette.title: Write The Follow-Up
etiquette.body: After any meeting that mattered: three lines confirming what was agreed and who does what. It prevents disputes and marks you as the reliable one. Almost nobody does it.
etiquette.action: Send a three-line recap after your next meeting.
etiquette.label: Etiquette

stillness.title: Solitude Is Not Loneliness
stillness.body: Solitude is time free of other minds' input. It is where thinking happens. A room full of people and a phone full of voices are the same interruption.
stillness.action: Take 30 minutes alone with no input. Not rest — thinking.
stillness.label: Stillness

model.title: Confirmation Bias
model.body: You will scrutinise disagreeing evidence and wave through agreeing evidence. Knowing this does not stop it. The only defence is to seek the counter-case deliberately.
model.action: Find the strongest argument against your current position. Steelman it.
model.label: Mental Model

drill.title: Mental Math: 1% Anchoring
drill.body: Compute 1% of a number, then scale. 1% of 847,000 is 8,470. So 3% is 25,410 and 0.5% is 4,235. Fluency here makes you visibly faster in meetings than people with better degrees.
drill.action: Ten numbers. Find 1%, 3%, and 15% of each. Under 60 seconds total.
drill.label: Drill

health.title: Alcohol Has No Healthy Dose
health.body: The J-curve was confounding — the abstainer group included the already-sick. Current evidence points to a linear dose-response for cancer risk from zero, and sleep architecture degrades from the first drink.
health.action: Count last week's units honestly. Not a judgement, a baseline.
health.label: Health

case.title: Dunzo Shutdown: Last Mile Lessons
case.story: Dunzo raised $240M, burned through it all on dark stores, rider salaries, and heavy subsidies. Shut down in 2024. Unit economics never worked.
case.lesson: Last-mile logistics is brutally hard. Before raising money, prove you can deliver profitably at small scale. Capital scales problems, not just success.

fpna.title: Contribution Margin
fpna.body: CM = Revenue – Variable Costs. Know your CM by product, by customer, by geography.

cfo.title: CFO Interview: Top 5 Questions
cfo.body: 1. What's your capital allocation philosophy? 2. How do you manage a cash crisis? 3. Describe a time you stopped a bad investment. 4. How do you build trust with the CEO? 5. Walk me through a fundraise or M&A you led. Practice until smooth.

money_hack.title: Expense Tracking
money_hack.body: Track every expense for 30 days. You will find ₹3–5K of invisible leaks.

dubai.title: Saudi pays more. Consider it.
dubai.body: Riyadh FP&A bands sit 15–25% above Dubai's for the same role, driven by Vision 2030 spending, and the tax position is the same. The trade is lifestyle and family logistics, not money.
dubai.targets: Also live: Qatar and Bahrain, both quieter and both hiring.
dubai.action: Add Riyadh to the search. The Dubai-only filter is a self-imposed pay cut.

desk.productivity: Build systems, not goals. Goals are outcomes; systems produce them.

father.title: Put the phone in another room
father.do: One 20-minute block a day with the phone physically out of sight.
father.why: Infants track gaze from very early. Divided attention is visible to her, and the research on 'still face' shows how quickly infants disengage when a caregiver's face goes flat.

father.title: Give her the spoon
father.do: Let her hold a second spoon while you feed her with the first.
father.why: It converts feeding from something done to her into something she participates in. Control over the process reduces resistance later, when refusal becomes a real phase.

life_wisdom.teaching: Extends beyond property to taking what was not freely given — credit, time, attention.
life_wisdom.apply: Attribute the idea to the person who had it, in the meeting, by name. Taking credit is the most common form and the least noticed.

life_wisdom.teaching: The fourth of the sublime states. Not indifference — full engagement without being destabilised by the outcome.
life_wisdom.apply: Judge the decision by the process you followed, not by how it turned out. A good decision with a bad outcome is still a good decision; conflating them is how you learn the wrong lesson.

speaking.title: Name then explain
speaking.drill: Practise five answers that open with the conclusion: 'No — and the reason is…'
speaking.why: Burying the verdict at the end forces the listener to hold everything in memory. Lead with it.

interview_tech.q: How do you close the books in five days instead of fifteen?
interview_tech.a: Move work out of the close. Accruals estimated from a model rather than waiting for invoices; reconciliations performed continuously rather than at month end; intercompany agreed on a cut-off calendar with a hard deadline and a default position if unresolved; fixed asset and depreciation runs automated; and reporting built on the ledger rather than rebuilt in Excel. The cultural half matters more than the technical half — a fast close requires accepting a materiality threshold below which you do not adjust.

interview_tech.q: A store does AED 12M revenue at 38% gross margin. Rent is AED 1.8M, staff AED 2.1M, other fixed AED 900K. Is it worth keeping?
interview_tech.a: Gross profit = 12 × 0.38 = AED 4.56M. Fixed costs = 1.8 + 2.1 + 0.9 = AED 4.8M. Store contribution = −AED 240K. It loses money — but do not close it on that number alone. Ask three things: is the rent a committed lease you pay whether or not you trade; what does the store contribute to online fulfilment and brand presence in that catchment; and what is the exit cost. A negative-contribution store with four years left on a non-cancellable lease is often cheaper to run than to close.

interview_soft.q: Tell me about a time you changed your mind after being convinced by someone junior.
interview_soft.a: This is a culture question about ego. Pick a real instance, name the person's role, describe the argument they made and why it was better than yours, and say what you did afterwards to make sure they got the credit. The best version includes what you changed structurally so junior challenge became normal rather than exceptional.

interview_soft.q: Why are you leaving your current role?
interview_soft.a: Never criticise the employer. Frame as pull, not push, and make it structural rather than personal: the scope you want next does not exist there in the timeframe you want it. If there is an obvious reason they will infer — a merger, a new boss, relocation — name it briefly and neutrally before they ask. Anything that sounds like a grievance transfers directly onto how they imagine you will talk about them.
